claims.text: Wear performance of high-entropy-alloy protective coatings is primarily governed by formation of an in situ nanocrystalline mixed-metal oxide tribolayer.
The oxide tribolayer dynamically heals and protects the coating surface during sliding contact.
The initial coating has a homogeneous elemental distribution.
The initial coating contains minimal pre-formed oxide phases.
Increasing oxygen availability from inert to moderately oxidizing conditions promotes formation and refinement of a nanocrystalline mixed-metal oxide tribolayer at the sliding interface.
Selective oxidation of multiple alloying elements rapidly produces a mixed-metal oxide layer under oxidizing conditions.
The fine nanostructure of the oxide layer enables it to heal and re-form at damaged sites.
The oxide tribolayer reduces direct metal-to-metal contact.
Reduced direct metal-to-metal contact decreases wear relative to an inert environment.
A protective oxide tribolayer does not form, or forms only minimally, in the inert baseline environment.
Oxidizing conditions will produce a lower wear rate than inert conditions.
Oxidizing conditions will produce a more uniform nano-oxide tribolayer than inert conditions.
Oxidizing conditions will produce a lower friction coefficient than inert conditions.
Minimal protective-oxide formation in an inert atmosphere results in higher wear rates.
The proposed mechanism holds over moderate oxygen partial pressures and operational temperatures.
At extremely low or high oxygen availability, or outside the typical operational temperature range, mechanisms other than protective tribolayer formation may dominate.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis states that oxide-tribolayer formation primarily governs wear performance, whereas the uncertainty field says it is unknown whether dynamic oxide formation is dominant over other mechanisms.
